extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners (biotechnology/biochemical arts)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a patent specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, for biotechnology claims (proteins, nucleic acids, antibodies, antisense oligonucleotides), including genus/species, percent-identity, and function-defined claim issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement (35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must show that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner analysis asks whether the disclosure (taken with the pre-existing knowledge in the art) would have led one of ordinary skill to conclude the applicant possessed the full scope of the claimed invention; examples conclude either 'satisfies' or 'fails' the written description requirement based on facts such as structural disclosure, functional limitations, and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession via disclosure of a representative species
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of a specific species (e.g., an amino acid sequence shown as SEQ ID NO: 3) can demonstrate possession of a broader claimed genus if that species is representative of the genus and shares structural features common to the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disclosed species embodies structural features shared by each member of the claimed genus, and those in the art would recognize that representativeness, a single species may suffice to show possession of the genus (Example 10). Predictability that other species will retain the function increases representativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims defined by percent identity represent partial structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting a protein or nucleic acid defined as 'at least X% identical' to a disclosed sequence represent only a partial structure (e.g., 95% or 85% identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because percent-identity claims leave unspecified which residues may vary, the specification must teach or otherwise enable recognition of which positions can change and still fall within the claimed genus or retain claimed function. Lack of teaching on which residues can vary may cause written description failure (Examples 10, 11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to teach which residues/positions can vary while retaining function
rubrics_metrics.description: For genus claims that allow variation (percent identity or variant lists), the specification should indicate which amino acids/positions may vary without losing the claimed activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no disclosure or art-recognized correlation identifying allowable substitutions (or functional domains), one of ordinary skill cannot determine which variants within the percent-identity genus retain the claimed function, leading to a written description failure (Example 10, Claim 3; Example 11A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure–function correlation increases sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosed correlation between structural features (e.g., domains, active site residues) and function provides information on which variants will retain activity and supports claiming a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples showing deletion studies or domain identification (binding/catalytic domains) and statements predicting effects of conservative vs non-conservative substitutions are persuasive evidence that a single species supports a genus (Example 11B). The degree of correlation required varies with the type of activity (structural proteins vs enzymatic/ligand activities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and level of ordinary skill in the art affect required disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The more predictable the relationship between structure and function (and the higher the skill in the art), the fewer representative species are required in the specification to show possession of a genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the art is routine and predictive (e.g., antisense design, use of genetic code/computational tools), disclosure of a single sequence may be sufficient; where predictability is low, more correlating information or examples are needed (noted across Examples 10–12). The number of species required is inversely related to skill level in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction to practice / actual exemplars strengthen written description
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of an actual reduction to practice (experimental data, sequences, deposited materials) for species within the claimed genus supports that the inventor possessed the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification discloses only a single species experimentally reduced to practice, claims to broader genera that include functionally defined variants may fail unless other correlating disclosure exists (Example 11, Example 13). Practice notes advise separate enablement analysis where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-only claiming requires structural support
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims framed principally by function (e.g., 'proteins that catalyze A→B') must be supported by disclosure linking structure to that function; merely claiming function across a broad set without structural correlation is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification discloses only one species that performs the function but does not teach which structural variations preserve the function, the written description fails for function-defined genus claims (Example 10, Claim 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of known art tools (genetic code, computers) can supply identification of sequence variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-existing knowledge such as the genetic code and computational sequence tools can enable identification of nucleic acid sequences encoding proteins with specified percent identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where such tools would have allowed one skilled in the art to enumerate sequences (e.g., list all nucleic acids encoding an amino acid sequence or those with X% identity), disclosure of the protein sequence may suffice to show possession of the nucleic-acid genus (Example 11 analyses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antisense oligonucleotide genus sufficiency based on target sequence and art-recognized correlations
rubrics_metrics.description: For antisense oligonucleotide claims complementary to an mRNA, disclosure of the mRNA sequence (full-length complement) and art-recognized correlations (accessible regions, Shine-Dalgarno targeting, GC-content considerations) can support possession of representative antisense species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because algorithms and empirical rules exist to predict antisense activity and the full-length complement is a predictable effective species, the specification may be sufficient even absent actual antisense sequences; routine screening methods disclosed in the specification further support sufficiency (Example 12).

rubrics_metrics.name: Antibody claims — adequacy of antigen disclosure and routine methods
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequately characterized antigen (e.g., purified antigen, amino acid sequence, physical/chemical properties) together with routine methods for producing antibodies may support claims to antibodies against that antigen even without disclosing antibody sequences or a deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those of ordinary skill in immunology consider antigen description plus established antibody production techniques sufficient to conclude possession of antibodies to that antigen (Example 13). Evidence of general antibody class/structure knowledge also supports this conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to antibodies across species require cross-species structural correlation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim encompasses antibodies binding a protein from multiple species, the specification must disclose shared structural features or correlations between species (e.g., murine vs human Protein X) to show possession of the broader genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional-only statements predicting human Protein X behavior, without sequence or structural evidence or correlation to murine Protein X, are insufficient to support antibodies to non-disclosed species; an antibody claim to a genus including other species can fail absent such cross-species data (Example 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial structural disclosure (e.g., '95% identical') vs complete structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of a partial structure (percent identity) provides partial information about the claimed molecules, but not which parts vary; the sufficiency of such recitation depends on whether the specification teaches how variation relates to structure and function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner analysis treats percent-identity recitations as partial structure requiring additional disclosure or art-knowledge to link variation to function; if the specification does not identify allowable variation or correlate structure to activity, written description may fail (Examples 10–11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-recognized substitution/exchange groups and empirical knowledge inform analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical knowledge—such as amino acid exchange groups, expected effects of substitutions on tertiary structure, and known limits of substitution tolerance—can inform whether the specification would have put one in possession of the claimed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical notes reference literature (e.g., exchange group concepts, Chothia & Lesk) to guide the examiner; such background may allow broader claims to be supported if the art would expect structure or function conservation under certain substitutions (Example 11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching methods of making/identifying claimed species matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of methods for making or identifying variants (e.g., protocols for producing antibodies, gene-walking, computational screening) supports the conclusion that the inventor had possession of representative species of the claimed genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification discloses preferred screening methods or routine production protocols, and such methods are sufficient for a skilled artisan to make/test members of the genus, written description is more likely satisfied (Examples 12, 13, 14).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional disclaimers or absence of functional limitation affect scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claims include or omit functional limitations (e.g., requiring catalytic activity or not) affects written description analysis; claims lacking functional limitations may encompass inert variants and require broader structural disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 10's Claim 2 lacked a functional limitation and thus encompassed variants irrespective of function—analysis focused on structural disclosure and whether the specification described a sufficient portion (95%) of the structure to show possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice note: separate enablement analysis where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The written description analysis here addresses only possession; enablement (whether the specification teaches how to make and use the full scope without undue experimentation) is a separate issue and should be considered independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document repeatedly notes that enablement issues are not addressed in these examples and that a separate rejection for nonenablement should be made when appropriate.
